We IC people just want to make friends and keep a safe distance. Isn’t this the most basic need? Society should pay more attention to us, establish more opportunities for mutual aid, and let collective care warm every corner.

Just because I was quarantined for 14 days after coming back from New York, I was fired immediately? This epidemic prevention policy simply treats ordinary people as cannon fodder! The United States claims to be free and democratic, but in the end it does not even have basic job security, and procedural justice is a joke. Isolation is for public safety, but who will bear the consequences of unemployment? If this system is not changed, the bottom class will always be sacrificed.

Look at the United States during this epidemic. A national philosophy that puts 'me' first is really harmful! The president is still spreading false news. Isn’t this taking everyone’s health as a trivial matter? Selfishness will only make the crisis worse. What we need is unity, 'our' strength. Don’t be deceived by those rhetoric anymore. It’s time to change this self-centered culture. Otherwise, how can we talk about fairness and justice?

My heart clenches when I read statements that question the reality of the disease. This is not just a medical issue, but also society’s attitude towards vulnerable groups. Disease is real and it is not anyone’s fault, but we often judge it with prejudice. Let’s change this cognitive framework and stop letting traditional ethics constrain our empathy. Every life deserves to be treated gently, not misunderstood and criticized.

The advice from the National Institutes of Health actually makes sense, that is, let everyone maintain daily hygiene habits, such as washing hands frequently. If the virus does spread in the United States, wearing a surgical mask is also a reliable protective measure. Behind this is the logic of procedural justice - follow official guidance and avoid confusion. From a technological perspective, a simple technology like masks can effectively monitor risks and reduce transmission. We must view these measures rationally and not be led astray by panic.

Seeing everyone discussing how to deal with the epidemic, I can't help but think of the days when I insisted on exercising. Back then, running every day made me feel stronger physically and calmer inside. Rather than relying on external measures, it is better to start from yourself and take your health into your hands. This is not only protecting yourself, but also a love and responsibility for life. Take action and you will find that small changes can bring huge power.

Is Trump’s move really awesome? Will it help the Democratic Party win the election? He allowed his supporters to regard the epidemic as a hoax, and as a result, one of his own people fell. Isn’t this self-destruction of the Great Wall? Also talking about 'making America smart again', I think it is making America stupid again! If this epidemic prevention policy is not changed, it will be over sooner or later. It's so ironic that traditional ethical standards are trampled under his feet.

Look at this pandemic and economic recession, the current government is simply adding fuel to the fire! They failed to handle the epidemic well, but they still expect to be re-elected? Stop dreaming, voters are not fools. The economy is about to collapse, but we are still clinging to the old policies. Isn't it obvious that we need to change people? Get out of office now, we need a leader who can truly respond to the crisis.

My colleagues in Florida and I have called for the continuation of the Trump administration’s anti-epidemic policies, which reflects the importance of policy stability. In a public health crisis, adhering to the existing legal framework ensures effective implementation of measures and avoids chaos. Logically, continuation of proven strategies is more reliable than frequent changes, which helps control the spread of the epidemic.

Seeing that this climate forum was postponed to July due to the epidemic, I think this is actually a wise decision. The epidemic disrupted plans, but postponement rather than cancellation shows that organizers are still insisting on climate action, but have just adjusted the time. From a social perspective, this ensures that more people can participate safely and avoids the injustice caused by hasty hosting. Logically, such a procedural extension is more responsible than outright abandonment, as climate issues cannot wait, but fair participation is also key.

After seeing the report of the first COVID-19 death case, I felt the need to analyze it calmly. The death of this immunodeficient man in his 50s after being transferred to a nursing home is sympathetic, but from a risk assessment perspective, he was in a high-risk group, reminding us that public health responses need to be based on objective data rather than emotions. Procedural justice requires us to deal with risk levels rather than blanket panic. From an individualistic perspective, everyone's risks vary greatly, and we should pay attention to individual circumstances rather than blindly pursue collective unity. This helps allocate resources more efficiently and avoid overreaction.

Look at the chaos of the epidemic in Central America. The government’s anti-epidemic measures are simply exposing the power game! With the first case in El Salvador and lockdowns in various places, the Vice President of Nicaragua also held a "Love in the Era of COVID-19" parade. Isn't this a joke about human life? The virus has torn the cracks between class and power even wider. The poor are struggling and the powerful are showing off. Stop whitewashing peace. When will this social injustice end?

Judging from the data, the current flu season in the United States has killed 8,200 people, and the risk of COVID-19 transmission is relatively low. This reminds us that public health policy should be based on actual risks, not panic. It is wise to maintain a stable cognition and avoid overreaction.

Looking at those videos from the early days of the epidemic, the chaos in New York and the Chinese-style blockade were simply a global farce. What about international cooperation? In the end, it's not all about working on their own and reinforcing the estrangement. Mandatory collective epidemic prevention is ostensibly for the overall good, but in fact it makes individuals breathless. Procedural justice? Don't be ridiculous, even basic human rights can be sacrificed for the sake of so-called 'just results'. This is not epidemic prevention. It is clearly a carnival of power. Stop using those rhetoric to fool people!

Thinking back to those days, my heart is beating even faster now. It felt like the world was falling apart, everything was hanging on the edge, and the fear was all too real. Fortunately, there was no chaos in the end, otherwise I wouldn’t have thought about it. This makes me cherish my current peace even more. Although it is just a personal experience, the dependence on order is really unforgettable.

At the beginning of the epidemic, I worked at O'Reilly Auto Parts, which was labeled 'essential' because I thought the risk was controllable. The result? From the elderly to the young, myocarditis, cognitive impairment, and stroke are all here! Where is the procedural justice? The government response was chaotic and the risks of medical technology were seriously underestimated. Stop using 'uncertainty' as an excuse. Regulation must be strengthened to protect ordinary people!

My colleague is serving in the military. After recovering from COVID-19, the doctor said his lungs were worse than those of a regular smoker and that he could no longer run long distances or lift weights. What is this? Non-death sequelae are completely ignored, where is the procedural justice? Does it only matter if you die? Public health supervision must be strengthened, and ordinary people should no longer be used as guinea pigs!

As a nurse, those days were a nightmare. Every day when I walk into the hospital, I look at the helpless eyes of the children outside the window. They don't understand why they can't hug their loved ones. When I come to work in the morning, I always wonder which colleague I will lose today. Healthy partners were falling one by one, and I was afraid I would be next. This is not just personal fear, but the entire system's neglect of individual rights. We frontline workers struggle with collective sacrifices without seeing a fair distribution of resources.

Every time I go home, I have to strip naked in the garage and isolate myself for fear of bringing the virus to my partner. He didn't know if I could survive. The fear and loneliness were really beyond words. This was not only physical torture, but also spiritual tearing, which made me deeply understand the fragility of individuals in the face of disasters. Social relations have been ruthlessly cut off in this way. We should be supporting each other, but we can only suffer silently from a distance. This kind of trauma cannot be repaired by simple procedural justice. What it requires is real care and change.

I worked in retail and the management sucked and the customers had no bottom line. Just because an out-of-warranty item cannot be returned, someone deliberately coughed on me and caused me to contract the new coronavirus. How is this procedural justice? Clearly condoning violence! Under the free market, low-level employees have become victims. The results are so unfair. If reforms are not carried out, who will still be willing to sacrifice their lives? Think about our colleagues in the hospital. They are even worse. What is wrong with this society?

Stop fooling people with those death numbers! The seriousness of COVID has been grossly underestimated, and the government’s propaganda to reopen the economy is simply ridiculous. The hospitals are full. How many people have to wait for hours even to have a heart attack because there are no beds? This is not an accident at all, it is an unfair distribution of resources caused by policy failure and a naked disregard for human life!

Asymptomatic early cases result in permanent lung, heart or brain damage in about 19% of people, which is no small feat. You might not notice a 10% drop in lung function until you're out of breath after climbing four flights of stairs. We weren't sure at the time whether the damage would accumulate or if the clotting problems would shorten life. This highlights the urgency of regulating public health risks – surveillance and prevention must be strengthened to avoid long-term health inequalities. Behind the data is the silent cost of countless individuals. We cannot wait until a crisis breaks out before taking action.

It's such an irony that COVID affects children so little that we're getting away with it. If it hurt children as much as it hurts the elderly, would those politicians still downplay it so lightly? It’s long past time to pay attention to children’s health instead of using the epidemic as a political bargaining chip. Stop pretending you can't see it. This society's neglect of vulnerable groups will sooner or later pay the price!

I saw that video in Italy, where a man desperately asked for help next to his sister’s body. The body lay there for a week without anyone caring about it. How is this emergency management? It's a system crash! Over in India, people are queuing up outside hospitals with oxygen tanks in their cars, waiting to die. How is the fairness in the distribution of medical resources like this? Stop pretending to be peaceful, these bloody realities are ironclad evidence of government incompetence and social injustice, and must be completely reformed, otherwise the tragedy will only happen again.

Seeing Quebec impose a curfew in response to the epidemic, I can't help but think of the elderly people who are forgotten in Spanish nursing homes. This scene is so heart-wrenching. Although the policy is gradual, it is at least trying to protect everyone, especially the most vulnerable groups. We cannot just shout slogans, we must take real actions to ensure that every life is truly respected and cared for.

Look at these news. Both the United States and Canada have reported a shortage of nursing workers, and even the military has to intervene. Isn’t this a naked system failure? The government shouts slogans all day long, but in the end it cannot even guarantee the most basic care for the elderly. Who will take care of those vulnerable groups? Stop whitewashing the peace, what we need is thorough reform, not empty talk about procedural justice!

Reading about this experience made my heart clench. My family spans the globe and my uncle was one of the first people to be mass buried in northern Italy. In New York, there were funeral cars parked near a friend's house, and the hospital was right next to it. We met in the park wearing masks, and the fear is still unforgettable. I immediately sent my frail family members out of the city just to protect them. This makes me question: Are the existing epidemic prevention measures really effective? Why do we always fix things after the fact? The safety of our families is more important than anything else, and this collective protection is our deepest desire.

When I saw reports of temporary hospitals being built in the UK, corpse trucks in Italy, and corpses being burned on the streets in India, I thought about it calmly. This actually exposed the vulnerability of the global fight against the epidemic. Compared with other countries, we have not reached that stage. Thanks to everyone's compliance with epidemic prevention procedures, the worst consequences have been avoided. Procedural justice is so critical in a crisis, ensuring a fair response rather than chaos.

Seeing those refrigerated trucks queuing up makes me so angry! With so many people dying every day in the United States, it’s like a repeat of 9/11. What is this epidemic prevention policy doing? If the government can't even arrange basic space, how can we talk about justice? Stop making excuses, this is clearly a systemic failure that must be completely reformed, otherwise the tragedy will only repeat itself.

Some people have selective amnesia. The epidemic has killed so many people, and hundreds of people are still dying every day. COVID-19 has left more people disabled, but everyone seems to have forgotten. This society's disregard for public health is simply ridiculous. Ecological protection is not a slogan, it is life! Stop kidding yourself, we need to completely change this perception, otherwise disaster will only happen again.

When I was 9 years old, the financial crisis broke out. I asked my dad: ‘We didn’t lose money, did we? ’ In the end, we still lost money. At that time, adults' troubles were like clouds in the sky, which seemed far away but could not be touched. Now think about it, isn’t COVID the same for many people? When I was young, I always felt that disaster was far away from me. It was not until it really came that I understood the feeling of powerlessness. This made me reflect that social crisis is not a numbers game, but a hurdle in everyone’s heart, reminding us not to be too naive.

When I read this passage, my heart clenched. The epidemic has shattered what should have been a solemn farewell - when my uncle died of cancer, there could only be 15 people at the funeral, and it was difficult for even close relatives to gather. Without the ceremony of everyone crying and hugging together, the sadness seemed to be locked in a corner. Sometimes I felt like he was alive in a daze. This is not only procedural injustice, but also a disregard for human needs. Collective mourning is not a formality, but the only way for us to heal.

As a white-collar worker, I thought working from home was only temporary, but I didn’t expect that the epidemic would completely change my life. When I saw in the news that the morgues were full and that Italian officials advised people not to get haircuts, saying that they would be buried in closed coffins anyway, I felt mixed emotions. This is not only a loss of personal freedom, but also a struggle for each of us under collective epidemic prevention. Why do measures always make people feel weak? Perhaps we need more understanding than cold rules.

As a doctor, I saw firsthand the collapse of the medical system: bodies piling up 12 hours a day, six days a week for months on end. My wife’s mother died amid visitation restrictions and she barely got to see her for the last time. Countless colleagues have left the industry and we still face staff shortages to this day. This is not an accident, but a systemic injustice. The distribution of medical resources is seriously imbalanced and must be fundamentally changed.

As a nurse, I survived the peak of three years in the city's emergency COVID-19 ward. The system collapsed three times, with the first wave being the most dangerous. We don’t even have enough PPE. The virus spreads through aerosols when doctors intubate, and some people died as a result. The shortage of CAPR equipment is not an accident, it is a systematic failure of resource allocation! Stop using 'temporary difficulties' as an excuse. Medical technology safety must be strictly supervised, otherwise we are risking our lives.

ICU nurses treat each other and cleaners are forced to disinfect with vinegar? This is a disgrace to the medical system! COVID causes fatal blood clots, pulmonary fibrosis, patients die from lack of oxygen, and life support becomes a decoration. Stop whitewashing the peace, where is the procedural justice? Technical regulation has failed to such an extent that it must be completely reformed, otherwise the next victim may be you and me.

I still remember crying when I got vaccinated in January 2021 - it was the first time in months that I felt safe. Our unit rescued 58 patients in an 80-bed ward that year. Every time I think about it, I firmly believe that true justice is not just empty talk about procedures, but real lives saved. This change gives us all hope.

It breaks my heart to see what my parents are going through as doctors during the pandemic. Dad went into battle without a mask, faced with an unknown virus, and watched helplessly as patients left one by one, colleagues fell down, and families could not be reunited. This exposes the unfair distribution of medical resources and urgently needs reform. But their collective dedication and perseverance against all odds moved me deeply. This spirit must be passed on.

I cried when I saw the ice rink in Spain turned into a morgue. My grandma, who is over 80 years old, is a cancer survivor. During the epidemic, we couldn’t even visit her. The numbers soared on TV every day, but she was alone at home. Is it fair that so many people are struggling on the verge of life and death just because of a lack of resources? We have to change this and stop putting families through this pain.

My heart clenched when I read this story. While my grandfather was in isolation in a nursing home, his neighbors left one by one. He could only repeatedly fold clothes, suffer from hallucinations, and even wish to die. This is not only a failure of the isolation policy, but also a trample on personal dignity. We always say that collective interests come first, but when the elderly have lost even basic spiritual comfort, is this collectivism still worth maintaining? It’s time to reflect and don’t let cold rules swallow up the warmth of humanity.

Reading this story made my heart clench. During the epidemic, family members were unable to visit, and even sending a flashlight failed. The feeling of powerlessness was too real. The most heartbreaking thing is that grandpa cried when he heard grandma's voice - after months of loneliness, he finally had some warmth. This reminds me that no matter how strict the policy is, it cannot cut off family ties. Family ties are what we should protect the most, right?

As an introvert, I’ve found my little blessings during the pandemic: working from home, tending my garden, and watching my one-year-old grow. But my heart clenches when I think about victims of domestic violence who are trapped in tiny apartments, their children without the protection of school. The contrast was unreal - my peace intertwined with their pain, a reminder that more changes are needed as a society to protect those who are most vulnerable.

My heart clenched when I read these words. The epidemic is like a ruthless pair of scissors, cutting our social ties into pieces. Smartphones and social media are supposed to bring us closer, but instead they become a catalyst for loneliness. Think of those closed gathering places. What was once bustling is now only a memory. My high school and college friends seem to have become the last resort. The weakening of this collective connection makes people wonder, can we still find that warmth? Behind the convenience brought by technology is deeper social isolation. Perhaps more supervision is really needed to protect the warmth between people.

Working remotely during the pandemic has been a lifesaver, allowing me to take care of my family. But it’s particularly painful to see educational inequality and the collapse of medical trust. My husband is a teacher and is always worried about bringing the virus home. The helpless feeling I felt when my child got sick is still unforgettable. This is not just a personal experience, it exposes social injustice and we need more changes to protect every family.

'Solidarity' after Brexit? What a joke! Those who shouted "Britain First" are fighting over a roll of toilet paper during the epidemic. I saw with my own eyes ambulances crashing and bodies piling up. How is this the glory of isolationism? It is clearly a collapse of social order! If the government fails to respond and ordinary people suffer, how fair is the result? Stop sugarcoating things, this stark reality is the best irony.

I witnessed with my own eyes the loss of more than a dozen lives in the support group, and the departure of young friends, but my Facebook is still full of cold-blooded assholes spreading fake news, calling it 'fake news'. The platform turns a blind eye to harmful content. This is not only a loss of morality, but also a secondary harm to the victims. Stop being deaf and dumb. Social media must be held accountable and regulated, otherwise it will become a breeding ground for lies and pain.

My heart clenches as I read the stories of those who have lost their lives or been left disabled by COVID-19. This is not a tragedy for one person, but a collective trauma for our entire society that is deliberately ignored by many. Some people still deny its existence, but the pain is real. We need to wake up from this dream and take on each other's responsibilities so that justice will no longer be absent. This is not only a change, but also a rebuilding of respect and hope for life.

The American media has been selectively blind during the epidemic. How ironic! Ordinary people stay at home and watch TV dramas, but doctors and nurses are struggling on the edge of collapse, and the morgues are full. HBO's "The Last of Us" touches on the truth a little bit, but the reality is a hundred times crueler than this. It’s time for the media to wake up and stop whitewashing peace and covering up the unfair distribution of medical resources!

My heart was broken when I read this news. When a family loses its breadwinner, leaving behind helpless children and a grieving wife, this should arouse the sympathy and support of the society. But just a week later, hospital security spread the lie that they were faking the death to defraud the government of funds. This is not just a loss of life, but a collapse of trust and empathy. When procedural justice is trampled upon and public integrity becomes a joke, what else can we believe in? Moral reconstruction is urgent. We need to awaken the forgotten kindness from the bottom of our hearts, return the system to justice, and restore warmth to society. This is not only change, but also hope for the future.

As a respiratory therapist, I have experienced firsthand the strain on the medical system during the pandemic. Hospital resources have been stretched to the brink of collapse, which made me reflect deeply: Why is our medical distribution so unfair? I sincerely hope to see changes before I retire so that every health care worker and patient can receive the care and resources they deserve. This is not only for us, but also for the fairness of the entire society.

My heart clenched when I read these descriptions. Medical staff cried in the lounge, and family members watched their loved ones pass away through the glass but were unable to hug them. This is not only a personal tragedy, but also a microcosm of the unfair distribution of resources in the entire society. We are short of even basic protective equipment and have to plan to share ventilators, which exposes the fragility of the public health system. As an ordinary person, I can’t imagine the despair of those moments, but we must call for change so that everyone can have equitable medical resources instead of struggling to survive in the crisis.

Those people who refused to wear masks and claimed it was a scam now know how to ask for help? What an irony! I watched the patient's blood oxygen drop to over 70 in the hospital, and we had no choice but to lower the alarm because there was nothing we could do. How is this a medical issue? It is clearly a lack of social responsibility! In the face of a public crisis, everyone should wake up and stop being selfish, otherwise who will save you next time?

As a former resident doctor, I have witnessed too many lives and deaths during the epidemic. Facing death every day, but seeing some people casually saying that the new coronavirus is fake, my heart was broken at that moment. I broke down and cried in the parking lot. I had nightmares again and again, but for the sake of the collective, we medical staff gritted our teeth and persisted. This is not only a personal sacrifice, but also the epitome of social injustice - indifference to the epidemic has overwhelmed the medical system. We need more substantive justice, not empty slogans.

When the epidemic was at its worst, it was really heartbreaking to see elderly patients admitted to the hospital every day, only to be unable to recover due to resource constraints. We medical staff try our best, but we still watch lives pass away. This is not only a matter of fairness in the medical system, but also a collective responsibility that the entire society needs to reflect on. The spirit of unity in fighting the epidemic is valuable, but if resource allocation is not reformed, the tragedy will happen again.

When I read these descriptions, my heart tightened - those 55-65 year olds who should have enjoyed family happiness, but died in pain due to insufficient medical resources. They are full of retirement plans, but they have become statistics, which nakedly exposes the injustice of society: why are some people able to be rescued in time, while others can only wait to die? What is even more tragic is that although medical technology seems advanced, it is unable to even provide basic respiratory support, and the regulatory system is full of loopholes. We must reform and no longer let lives disappear in despair. This is not only a technical problem, but also a test of human nature.

My heart clenched when I read these stories. The patient who struggled on pure oxygen, the son who inadvertently brought the fatal virus to his father at the birthday party, and the mother who refused life-saving medicine but forgot that she had benefited from it - these are not only medical choices, but also a torture of the dignity of life. We always talk about individual freedoms, but when public health is at stake, shouldn’t we prioritize protecting the most vulnerable? These tragedies remind us how important traditional medical authority and timely intervention are, and don’t let stubbornness destroy more families.

It makes me feel bad to see that everyone's respect for the medical profession is getting weaker and weaker. Think about those doctors and nurses, they have paid so much, but there are always some people who are self-righteous and point their fingers. They dare to question their profession without even studying high school science well. This generation of medical workers is really tired, but I believe that the new generation will bring changes and make this field full of hope and vitality again.

As a CNA, I have been working on the front line since the beginning of the epidemic. The protective mask was so corroded by bleach that it was almost invisible. After six months of use, I had to tilt my head to see the patient. In the first few months, all the patients either died or were admitted to the ICU and never came back. This exposes the failure of procedural justice in the medical system, the unfair distribution of resources, and the chilling lack of supervision. Stop fooling people with empty words, we need real reforms to keep health care workers and patients safe!

My heart clenched when I read this. As a former health care worker, I know the feeling of helplessness - the sirens blaring, one person caring for 40 patients, and the onslaught of COVID dementia patients. This is more than just a personal sacrifice, it exposes a deep injustice in the health care system: resources are so unevenly distributed that we, the frontline workers, are like forgotten pawns. If society fails to provide adequate support, this tragedy will only happen again. I hope more people see that change is imminent.

7 million confirmed deaths worldwide? The actual excess deaths exceeded 15 million! In 2020-21, hospitals were overcrowded and COVID-19 left millions of people disabled. Stop talking about individual risk differences, this is simply a systemic failure! Where is the social justice? When public health is so fragile, how can we prioritize development? There must be radical changes, and protecting life comes first!

Official data is always just the tip of the iceberg! That 6-year-old child died of diabetes, and a colleague fell ill with cancer. Behind these tragedies are the invisible harms of COVID. Stop fooling people with those whitewashed numbers. We need more transparent public health reporting and strict medical supervision, otherwise the next victim may be you and me.

My dad got diabetes after COVID-19, and he had no risk factors before! Two years later, 30 blood clots were found in my legs. Is this just a coincidence? Research on the sequelae of COVID-19 lags behind. The medical community is still using the same old diagnosis methods, which cannot cover these new problems at all. Where is the medical equity? Ordinary people's right to health has been ignored, and supervision must be strengthened to prevent more people from being harmed!

I will never forget April 2020, when my roommate contracted COVID in New York. She was only in her early 30s, healthy and lively, but she left us after struggling on a ventilator for a month. During that dark period, the lockdown measures were difficult, but they did save countless lives. Now think about it, COVID-19 is still tormenting many people. Wearing a mask in crowded places is really nothing. We need to put health first and not let economic priorities destroy more families.

It broke my heart to read the story of my roommate who passed away from COVID-19. He worked so hard and was a talented musician, but his kidneys and respiratory system were destroyed due to two infections. Some people say that death from COVID-19 is 'survival of the fittest', but how can life be measured by such an indifferent collective view? He is a living person with dreams and warmth who should not be forgotten in a programmed manner. This made me reflect, is our society too lacking in respect for every individual when dealing with the epidemic? Public health incidents should not focus only on numbers and ignore the pain and justice behind them.

I work in a 50-bed hospital, and I was originally handling non-COVID-19 surgeries, but I was overwhelmed by the epidemic. The 5-bed orthopedic ICU was abruptly changed to a new coronavirus ICU. The nurses learned while doing it and relied on online module training? That's ridiculous! This is not an emergency, it is clearly a joke with human life. The policy deployment is chaotic and the training procedures are ineffective. If we don’t reform, what can we expect when the next disaster strikes?

Look at this medical chaos! When recovering from elective surgery, people are sent home after outpatient procedures, and there are not even beds for complications. Hip replacement, hysterectomy, or even amputation, same-day discharge? The result? Complications such as hematoma, fractures, and blood transfusions occur frequently. The PACU and preoperative area have become COVID-19 isolation areas. Isn't this a joke on human lives? Where is the procedural justice? Supervision is ineffective and must be completely reformed. Don’t let patients pay for loopholes in the system!

As an older person with health issues, it breaks my heart to read the words 'Only the sick are dying'. It's not just numbers, it exposes the cruelest side of society: we are treated as disposable pawns so that others can 'get back to normal'. Is this how the value of life should be ranked? This reminds me of those forgotten corners. We need to change this injustice so that every life is respected and not sacrificed on the altar of collective interests.

I am 31 years old and very healthy. Three weeks after getting mild symptoms of COVID-19, I suddenly fainted after walking a few steps. I was diagnosed with pulmonary embolism and heart problems and almost had surgery. This is not a trivial matter at all. COVID-19 has caused blood clots among young people, but the media and public health system are covering it up. Where are the risk warnings? The lack of procedural notification is simply treating human life as a child's play! The public monitoring system must be strengthened to prevent more people from being victimized.

I feel particularly sad when I see friends of the same age around me who are still suffering from COVID-19, and some elders who have passed away because they underestimated the epidemic. This epidemic has exposed health inequities, and not everyone has the same opportunities for protection. Fortunately, my family has always protected me. This is what they should do and it is also a tradition that our society should uphold. I hope this inequality can be changed in the future so that every family can be safe.

Bodies have been lying in refrigerated trucks in New York for months, and the medical system has collapsed like this. Why are officials still warning about heart attacks and bicycle accidents? This is a travesty! Hospitals are overloaded and resource allocation is in a mess, and they still haven’t recovered. Stop pretending to be peaceful, this injustice must be reformed, otherwise ordinary people will not be able to secure even basic medical care.

The allocation of medical resources has actually reached the point where we have to choose who lives and who dies? This is simply a naked irony! Stop talking about procedural justice. When people are turned away because they are 'not sick enough', where is the justice in the results? Policy reform is urgent, and we need more equitable distribution, rather than letting lives become a bargaining chip.

Looking back at the early stages of the epidemic, WHO's rapid coordination and international cooperation were crucial, which reflected the globalist diplomatic strategy. Lockdown measures such as New Zealand's decisive action, although a little late, prevented mass deaths and proved the concept of just results - saving lives is the last word. Data doesn’t lie, and this kind of evidence-based decision-making is worth pondering.

As a former Texas teacher, I have a fragile immune system during the epidemic, but I persisted in teaching in hybrid classrooms. Every Friday, I call students’ families and listen to them. Once, a mother told me that her son was unable to go to school because he had lost two uncles and brothers in one week. This trauma is all too common, and it made me deeply aware of the fragility of the education system in a crisis, but it also highlighted the power of collective care - we are all trying to support each other, not only to teach, but to protect humanity.

Some people are still pretending to be stupid, saying that the new coronavirus is not a big deal and has been covered up? Is the global shutdown a joke? How ironic that Trump and his fans are making a fool of millions of lives for the sake of the economy! The government's intervention in the economy and forced blockade are necessary measures to save lives, not to harm you. The collective responsibility for epidemic prevention is higher than individual freedom. Don't always think about your own petty calculations. Epidemic information transparency? Haha, if it weren't for the questioning voices, more people might still be in the dark. Wake up, this is not a game, it is a matter of life and death!

The words of the Texas Lieutenant Governor are simply chilling. How do you say that the elderly must die financially to survive? Isn't this kind of naked disregard for life just using procedural justice as a shield? During the epidemic, many policies only focus on economic figures, but forget that human lives are at stake! Stop fooling us by saying 'the overall situation is the most important thing'. This is simply moral decay. We must completely change this cold-blooded logic. The right to life should always take priority.

Stop using 'science is progressing' as an excuse! Those in power are watching the data update while inciting distrust in experts. Isn't this a blatant violation of consensus? Procedural justice? It has expired a long time ago. Ordinary people were deceived into 'researching' it on their own. What's the result? Hospitals are full of people who are living with regret and relying on crowdfunding to save their lives. The scientific communication mechanism is so rotten. If supervision is not strengthened, the next victim may be you and me.

These so-called 'experts', like chiropractors and notorious doctors, know how to promote unproven treatments, accept cash only and not accept insurance, and are using their patients as cash cows! If something goes wrong, it would be better for them to put all the blame on the patient and say, "You didn't persist." This kind of lie exploits people's fears and erodes our trust in formal medical care bit by bit. The distribution of medical resources is already unfair enough, and they are adding fuel to the fire. This chaos must be completely rectified, and innocent people cannot be harmed anymore!

Breakthroughs in genetic sequencing technology are the key to rapid vaccine development, which is a reflection of the inclusiveness of science and technology. Think about it, without these innovations, how much more would the death toll from the epidemic have soared? It has literally saved countless lives and demonstrated the value of technical freedom and fair outcomes.

Every time I see someone not wearing a mask, I think of my friends who are still fighting Long Covid. This is not alarmist. The epidemic is far from over. It is like an invisible knife, quietly hurting our body and future. We must act to protect ourselves and others, not just as a personal choice but as a commitment to justice in life. Let us protect our health together and don’t let negligence become a regret.

The selfishness of Americans is really speechless! Some people complain about small things like wearing masks and complying with lockdown orders, as if they are wronged. My colleagues complain about the mask requirement every day. The law clearly requires it, but they turn a deaf ear to it. What’s even more ironic is that a surgeon died due to the epidemic, and his family held a super-spreading funeral. What's wrong with this society? Collective responsibility was forgotten and legal enforcement was ineffective. Stop making excuses. This kind of selfish behavior will only harm others and yourself. We must strengthen the enforcement of public health laws, otherwise the tragedy will happen again.

During the epidemic, I was doing property restoration, and a property owner coughed directly into my face because I didn’t take off my mask. What is this? Where is the procedural justice? The rules clearly require wearing masks to protect everyone, but some people only care about their own comfort and take the safety of others as a joke. This kind of extreme individualism is rampant, which is really infuriating! Has social responsibility been fed to the dog? We need reform to stop allowing this kind of selfish behavior to run rampant.

It really breaks my heart to see those who are against wearing masks. Wearing a mask is just a small gesture, but it can protect everyone. Why do they have to say it is an infringement of freedom? What’s even more sad is that the Asian community has encountered hatred and even violence because of their compliance with mask regulations. This is not just a matter of individual choice, but whether we as a society are willing to make sacrifices for the collective good. Inconsistent policies only add fuel to the fire, and we need to focus on actual results, not empty procedures.

I'm really convinced, can such a small thing as a mask cause such a big fuss? Isn't it just a piece of cloth? To protect the health of others, does it have to be political? Look at those people who accept car registrations and home loans, but double standards when it comes to public health, it's ridiculous. Collective interests should not be hijacked by individual freedom. Justice in the outcome is the key. Don't let hypocrisy ruin everyone's health.

Look at these selfish people who refuse to wear masks during the epidemic. They are simply making fun of other people's health! Those rumors are flying all over social media, which makes people even more angry. This is not personal freedom, it is clearly a lack of collective responsibility. History repeats itself, but this time it's worse because ignorance is amplified. Stop making excuses, protecting everyone is the right way!

I will never forget the constantly running crematoriums and morgue trucks on the streets in New York. People took off their clothes when entering to isolate themselves from the virus. That kind of fear was engraved in the hearts of countless people. But some people insist that this is a conspiracy and deny the danger, which makes me heartbroken. Our shared trauma should not be forgotten, and it reminds us that in the face of crisis, collective memory and truth are the starting point for healing.

Those days in Kew Gardens, Queens, New York, were truly unforgettable. The sirens are blaring all the time, and the streets are empty, like a forgotten ghost town. Supermarket shelves are often empty, and we have to make our own masks out of old T-shirts, just to leave medical supplies for those who need them more. Garbage piled up, green spaces grew wildly, work tripled, and half of our colleagues were forced to lose their jobs. At 7 o'clock every night, we stood in front of the window on time and applauded the medical staff fighting on the front line. At that moment, I deeply felt that in the crisis, we can still unite and protect each other's warmth. This is not just survival, but a silent commitment to the public good.

That day in New York, I witnessed ambulances parked three buildings outside. After the death of a neighbor, the body waited for nine hours before being taken away. The book friend cried and told me that a refrigerated truck was parked near her home, loaded with the deceased. But when I told my relatives in rural Texas, they said I was making it up. This is not only a failure of the emergency system, but also a tear in our social values ??- why is personal experience so easily dismissed? We need to reexamine these injustices so that everyone’s voice is heard.

When I lost my father and my aunt, there were long lines of refrigerated trucks in our town, and neighbors were leaving one by one. As a 9/11 lung disease survivor, I got vaccinated as soon as possible, just to grab any shred of protection. Now, the nanny is still fighting against COVID-19, so I choose to educate my children at home so that they can see the cruel truth of this world. How much social injustice has the epidemic exposed? We can no longer be silent and must drive change to ensure everyone has equitable access to health care. Technology supervision is not a constraint, but a bottom line to protect life.

As an ICU nurse, those days are truly unforgettable. We built a new ICU overnight, and young people were busy operating ventilators and even turning patients into prone positions to improve lung function - something that was rarely done before. Everyone wrote their needs on the glass of the room. The air was filled with sweat and fear, but the light of teamwork was particularly dazzling. This made me deeply realize that in a crisis, procedural justice and collectivism are not empty slogans, but the hope that each of us protects with action.

Look at this data: One million Americans have died from COVID-19, hospitals are full, and even patients with heart attacks and strokes cannot receive timely treatment. This is not an accident, it is a systemic injustice in the distribution of medical resources! COVID-19 and cardiopulmonary sequelae are still tormenting people, and it was even worse when there was no vaccine. Stop whitewashing the situation, public health technical supervision must be strengthened, otherwise the next disaster will only be worse.

Every time I see someone taking the COVID-19 lightly, I feel uncomfortable. These are not just numbers, they are real people! We must shoulder the responsibility together, strengthen education, and let everyone understand the risks of transmission and the dangers of COVID-19. This is not the end, but a time for more care.

When I read this passage, my heart clenched. The epidemic stole my college time. From enrollment to lockdown, in just five months, my youth changed. There is no study abroad, internships are cancelled, and even classes have become pixels on the screen. Our generation should have been colliding and growing up in reality, but we were forced to be isolated. Those experiences that cannot be repeated are like dreams blown away by the wind. I often wonder where I would be without this chaos? Young lives should not be interrupted so easily. This is not only a pity, but also a torture of fairness.

COVID-19 is still dangerous, we are just learning more. Vaccines, medicines and masks do work, but many people ignore them. Living with COVID-19 can cause POTS, lung problems, and brain fog. This is no small thing, it’s real brain damage. Even asymptomatic infection can spread the virus. The logic is simple: getting up to date on your vaccinations and wearing a mask in crowded places are basic steps to protect yourself and others. Don't wait until you regret it before taking action. Health is not a child's play.

As someone who has insisted on wearing masks for a long time, it is really sad to see people ignoring protective measures. Vaccines are not a panacea and cannot completely prevent transmission or long-term sequelae, but masks and improved air quality are key to protecting everyone. We cannot only focus on the convenience of a few people while ignoring the health rights of vulnerable groups. Think about those people living in a polluted environment, who will protect their health? It’s time to put environmental health first and strengthen public health supervision so that everyone can breathe clean air. This is true fairness.

My heart breaks when I read those cold death figures. I lost three relatives, the hospital was empty, and I couldn’t even see them for the last time. This is not a simple statistic, but the destruction of countless families. Why is our pain downplayed? Society should remember these and bear this pain together instead of letting them pass away in the wind.

As a veterinarian, those days gave me a deep understanding of the complexity of human nature. We once put a dog on a ventilator, and its owner was fighting COVID-19 in the same hospital. This connection of lives moved me. But on the other side, some people are yelling about cutting their nails, refusing to wear masks, and completely disregarding the safety of others. What is even more heartbreaking is that the clinic lent its equipment to people for use in the hospital, resulting in the death of many animals due to lack of medical care. This is not only a misallocation of resources, but also a lack of collective responsibility. We could have done better, couldn't we?

As a nurse, I have experienced the baptism of the COVID-19 epidemic. The daily deaths, shortage of protective supplies, and patient denial have left deep scars in my heart. This is not my story alone, but the shared trauma of our entire medical community. It has exposed the fragility of the public health system, but it has also brought us closer together. We may never go back to where we were before, but this experience shapes our identity and reminds us of the need for change.

As a person with a weak immune system, I lived in fear every day during the early days of COVID-19, fearing that I would lose everything if I got infected. Seeing people voluntarily sewing masks to support medical care, the solidarity made me cry. When the vaccine was developed, it was like a ray of light in the darkness. I witnessed long lines at vaccination sites, everyone yearning for that safety. This is not only a breakthrough in technology, but also a manifestation of social fairness - everyone should have equal opportunities to be protected, instead of being forgotten in the corner.

My wife is immunocompromised and every time she goes out to buy groceries or work, she is walking on a tightrope for fear of bringing the virus home. It breaks my heart to see some people crazily opposing epidemic prevention measures. This is not about making a mountain out of a molehill, but about protecting vulnerable people like us. Their selfishness made this difficult time even worse. We are a society, shouldn’t we think more about others?

That day, I was driving for vaccination at the county fair. The car wound between cattle pens, and nurses handed out injections from the car window. Although the scene was a bit surreal, it warmed my heart. I felt that everyone was united and had hope of regaining a normal life. It’s more than just a shot, it’s a microcosm of our community supporting each other in the midst of chaos, giving credence to the power of collective action.

Every time I see those who have lost their lives indirectly due to the epidemic, my heart tightens. Delays in cancer screenings, surges in domestic violence, shortages of medical resources—there are real people behind these numbers! We can no longer just focus on direct death data. We must redefine statistical standards to make society more just. At the same time, the public health crisis reminds us that protecting human health means protecting the ecology. Only by prioritizing the environment can we avoid the next disaster. This is not only a change, but also a respect for life.

My father refused to be vaccinated and eventually contracted COVID-19 because a colleague came to work while sick. He died alone at the age of 77. He could have lived a few more years, but his time was taken away by selfish actions. I was unable to visit in the hospital, and this pain was not only a personal tragedy, but also the epitome of social injustice. When individuals choose to endanger public health, who will protect the innocent and vulnerable? We must reflect and pursue a fair outcome so that every life can receive the respect and protection it deserves.

As an asthmatic, COVID-19 made me cough like broken glass, and that fear is still unforgettable. Seeing the 20% mortality rate among 80-year-olds and the loss of 600 lives in the entire community, I worry about my elderly parents day and night. It wasn't until the vaccine came out that I felt a little more at ease. This made me deeply realize that society must give priority to protecting vulnerable groups and ensure fairer public health; scientific and technological supervision must be stricter, and saviors like vaccines cannot make any mistakes. Otherwise, how can we protect the people we love?

Look at this shit! The governor of Maryland had to secretly transport protective equipment from South Korea and had to bring armed guards, but Trump was grabbing supplies to please the Republican governor and take credit. This is simply a textbook case of political corruption. In times of crisis, they only care about playing power games and treating ordinary people's lives as trivial matters. Stop saying that 'the system is fine'. This unfair distribution of resources nakedly exposes the failure of the system, which must be completely reformed, otherwise we will suffer the next disaster.

Thinking back to the early days of the pandemic, the fear of the unknown was truly suffocating—every doorknob seemed like a hidden threat. We work in an electrical appliance wholesale store, and the company's instructions are not taken into account at all. Everyone voluntarily implemented a "telephone pick-up" to protect employees. Supermarket shelves are emptied and streets are empty. In that chaos, our small changes bring a sense of security. This is not only a response to a crisis, but also a flashback of human nature under pressure, reminding us that society needs more such independent actions to protect each other.

When I was eight months pregnant, the lockdown policy made me anxious every day, fearing that my mother who worked in a pharmacy or my husband who was an essential service worker would bring the virus home. Later, I was hospitalized repeatedly due to kidney failure, a total of 35 times, and I was never able to have my family by my side. The loneliness still makes me sad when I think about it. After the child was born, my husband's anti-vaccination relatives actually threatened to file a lawsuit to fight for 'ancestral rights'. The epidemic is like a mirror, revealing the deep-rooted rifts in the family - when individual rights to health collide with the so-called 'collective interests of the family', the most vulnerable are always injured. This is not just my story, it reminds us that those old family relationship systems really need to be changed.

As an intensivist, the days of COVID-19 are truly unforgettable. I told my wife in advance that I would be needed. In the previous waves of the epidemic, despite our best efforts, many patients died after being put on ventilators and dialysis. The family members can only say goodbye on the phone, and the feeling of powerlessness is so heart-wrenching. For the safety of my family, I haven’t seen my children for several months and work 12 hours a day wearing an N95 mask. This is not only a professional responsibility, but also our medical staff's persistence in collective interests and protecting the dignity of life in crises.

Seeing pictures of children wearing masks makes my heart clench. It was such a hard time and I pray we never have to go through it again. The vaccine has certainly helped a lot, but the enforcement measures have made me miss my previous free life. Is it fair that children’s smiling faces are obscured? We should think more about the actual impact of these policies on the next generation.

COVID-19 is not over at all! COVID-19 has become the number one chronic disease in children, and even asthma has been sidelined. The risk of repeated infection is high, half of the people are asymptomatic, and testing is completely useless. Isn’t this self-deception? Wearing a mask in public is basic protection, but some people just refuse and ignore the health of others. Brain fog is brain damage, stop trying to excuse it by saying 'it's okay'. We need enforcement to protect the weak, not laissez-faire. Detection technology must be improved, stop fooling people with invalid tools!

I got COVID-19 in the summer, and now I still have dizziness, fast heartbeat, and brain fog. I’m really getting over it! The death rate has dropped, but more and more people are being disabled by COVID-19 for a long time. Some people still pretend that the disease has passed. Isn’t this lying? The public health risks are so obvious, but the government and society turn a blind eye. Supervision must be strengthened to prevent more people from suffering!

These days of the epidemic are not too bad for me - I stay at home and save toilet paper, I lost my job but found a better one. But every time I think about friends losing loved ones, medical staff suffering trauma, and those suffering from COVID-19, my heart becomes filled with panic. Fate is really playing tricks on people. I am grateful for my luck, but I can't help but worry about the suffering of others. This makes me understand better that there is no absolute fairness in life, but at least we can have more understanding and care.

Reading those reports about Long Covid makes my heart clench. It’s not just brain fog or loss of taste, there are countless people suffering mental breakdowns in silence, struggling alone in isolation. It’s not just a health issue, it exposes social injustice – why do some people have better support while others face it alone? We must change this situation so that everyone can find warmth and hope in the crisis.

While working in the ICU, I witnessed too many lonely deaths. Those Zoom farewells using iPads were supposed to be the last hugs of family members, but instead they became cold screen interactions. This is not what the medical system should be like. It exposes the unfair distribution of resources and allows individual dignity to disappear in the collective interests. We must change this system so that everyone can feel warm and respected at the end of their lives.

Stop pretending the pandemic is the same for everyone! While remote workers stay safe at home, workers at the bottom risk their lives—a stark reminder of the unfair distribution of privilege and risk. Unequal opportunities directly lead to unfair results, and economic distribution is like a scam. Why can some people be comfortable while others have to sacrifice everything? It’s time to completely change this twisted system!

As a medical staff, the days of COVID-19 are truly unforgettable. Watching life go by every day, my aunt passed away in just five days. Those who deny the epidemic have never seen the bodies piled up in hospitals with their own eyes. This kind of disregard is so chilling. What we need is not arguments, but real actions to protect everyone and prevent tragedies from happening again.

During the epidemic, I worked from home and thought I could escape. But in just seven months, six of my relatives passed away. My sister now has to rely on crutches to walk, and the other one has even lost her sense of taste. At night, I often dream about the missed funerals and the suffering in the ICU. How is this a personal tragedy? It is the injustice of the entire society that is causing trouble! We need to unite and show more collective care, and stop letting families bear this pain alone.

I've been through Columbine, 9/11, and the recession, but COVID-19 is really different. Entire industries were shut down, trucks were piled with bodies on the streets, and I was crushed by the endless lockdown. Later, I returned to work and worked on the front line. I was lucky enough not to be infected, but I watched the elderly customers suffer - they couldn't buy medicine, they didn't dare to go out, and they were like a forgotten corner. Is this blanket blockade really reasonable? The economy has stopped and people's hearts are broken. Only those who have experienced it can understand the pain of being deprived of freedom.

Reading about this experience made my heart clench. We have to reuse N95 masks and disinfect them in paper bags, which are supposed to be disposable. My colleague was intubated and we had to pass notes through the hospital pipes. Every day when I came home, I would take off my clothes at the door and rush into the bathroom, for fear of bringing the virus to my children. This exposes the unfair distribution of medical resources. There is an urgent need to strengthen supervision on the use of protective technology. Frontline personnel can no longer be allowed to take such risks.

In Bergen County, my heart broke when I saw the refrigerated trucks outside the hospital. A colleague of the same age just passed away. That kind of fear made me dare not see my family for several months for fear of harming them. While others are ignoring this crisis, we are fighting for each other's lives. This is not only isolation, but also a silent protection of collective safety. Why do some people just don’t understand this pain?

As an oncology nurse, I was heartbroken by the wave of chemotherapy patients in March 2020, many of whom never returned. Later, I was transferred to the COVID-19 transition ward. BiPAP was the hope of life, but intubation meant goodbye. The loneliness and exhaustion of rescuing patients every night and being isolated after being infected are unforgettable. This is not only a personal sacrifice, but also the epitome of our collective perseverance in medical care - amidst resource constraints, we silently shoulder our responsibilities just to protect every life.

As a nurse who has worked for 20 years, I will never forget the three months from March to May 2020. More people are dying than in a normal year, young and healthy patients are gasping for breath, and the elderly are being denied ventilators as resources are prioritized for those who are likely to survive. We even had to use masks over and over again. The helplessness made me want to give up. This is not a simple mistake, it is a breakdown of the entire system. We need radical changes so that everyone can get treatment fairly and not be abandoned by cold rules.

As an ICU nurse, I will never forget that scene: an old couple shared a ventilator, and their lives were swaying in the struggle. The patient resisted treatment and the threats from his family members made me heartbroken about the fragility of human nature. This is not a simple medical problem, but a lack of social justice, where our collective values ??collapse under extreme pressure. We need to deeply reflect on why the distribution of resources is so unfair and why does love become distorted in crises? This is not only a time for change, but an opportunity to awaken empathy.

读到这个家庭悲剧，我的心都碎了。 My father was infected with COVID-19 and died after attending my sister’s Thanksgiving party. Nine people were diagnosed and four were hospitalized. This is not only the fault of the virus, but also the neglect of traditional family responsibilities. As children, we are supposed to protect our families and not let the party turn into a disaster. It is necessary for the law to hold people responsible for transmission, and it reminds us that during the epidemic, everyone must be responsible for their own actions. I hope this lesson can alert more people and stop letting family relationships be ruined by negligence.

As an ICU nurse, COVID-19 has completely devastated me. Ten years of intensive care experience pales in face of life and death every day. I eventually left the bedside, not because I didn’t love the job, but because the injustice of the system left me unable to breathe. Now, every time I think about returning to that environment, the nights become long. This is not only my personal choice, but also a silent cry for reform of the medical system.

2020 is simply a wake-up call! From the pandemic to the Floyd protests to the raging wildfires, this is not just a coincidence, but a total outbreak of social injustice and ecological crisis. We must radically change this systemic problem and we can no longer sit back and do nothing! The time to take action to protect our planet and pursue true justice is now!

As a laboratory scientist, I process hundreds of COVID-19 tests every day as doctors and nurses anxiously await the results. Shortages of protective supplies have led to frequent thefts and the exodus of respiratory therapists and nurses. We work 12-hour shifts and stick to our posts, only to see deniers calling the epidemic a hoax and helplessly watching young people in their 30s pass away. This is not only work, but also a manifestation of collective dedication. However, the unfair distribution of medical resources and chaotic management require urgent reforms and strengthened supervision to protect more lives.

It’s really chilling to look at what happened during the epidemic. Wearing a mask, a basic protective measure, has been used as a political bargaining chip by some people, who have ridiculed death and bullied nurses. How is this simple selfishness? It is clear that the entire system condones lies and betrayal. Political elites are willing to sacrifice the lives of ordinary people for votes. This kind of corruption is deeply rooted. Stop talking about procedural justice. When the rules are being played, what else can we believe? This ultra-individualistic culture must be radically changed, otherwise society will only become increasingly divided.

Stop using the epidemic as an excuse! The rich have doubled their wealth by relying on stocks and real estate, while the poor are struggling with inflation and do not even have basic assets. How many people are forced to retire early due to the collapse of the medical system? Children spend all day on social media and don’t even know how to communicate face to face. How could this be an accident? It is clearly a magnifying glass for the injustice of the system! We must push for change and stop allowing this division to continue.

The school’s epidemic prevention policy is in vain! The new coronavirus not only activates cancer and breaks through the blood-brain barrier, but also destroys the immune system and damages organs even in mild cases. COVID-19 has become the number one chronic disease among children, yet we still allow it to spread in schools. How is this an oversight? This is a clear disregard for the health of the next generation! Reforms must be made immediately to strengthen protection measures and stop letting bureaucracy harm children.

As someone who experienced Omicron first hand, I will never forget the feeling of suffocation, like your throat was filled with shards of glass. For a whole year, I struggled to breathe, relying on an inhaler to survive. But the vaccine gave me a second chance at life and saved me from a worse outcome. Consider that the 1918 flu killed 50 million people, but this time through masks and vaccines, we only lost about 7 million – isn’t this a victory for public health measures? It is not just a number, it is the hope of countless families. We must persist with this proactive intervention to ensure everyone has equitable access to protection and not make health a luxury. Technical supervision is not a constraint, but a protection. It allows science to truly serve people.

My heart clenched when I read this story. My daughter’s dad once mocked COVID-19 as a conspiracy until he lost his sense of taste, coughed non-stop, refused medical treatment, and was gone two weeks later. This is an avoidable tragedy with simple protection. What makes me even more sad is that my neighbors and friends are also falling ill one after another. This is not just a matter of personal choice, it is about the responsibility of each of us - if we do not put collective epidemic prevention first, how many innocent lives will be lost? It’s time to reflect, and for a just outcome, we must act.

When I worked in the state health department, I processed tens of thousands of COVID-19 test faxes every day, with names, ages, death records... The grief of those strangers still makes it difficult for me to let go. I built automated systems to speed up data processing and help with contact tracing, but despite my best efforts, the psychological scars still lingered. This is not to question the system, but to let everyone see that in a crisis, technology and personal efforts are all for stabilizing and protecting lives.

From a scientific perspective, repeated Covid infections do increase long-term health risks, reminding us of the need for technical regulation. Mandatory mask orders and air filtration measures have played a key role in the epidemic, but without legal enforcement, public compliance will be greatly reduced. Thinking about the lessons of HIV and polio, why is it now being treated like seasonal flu? The logical loopholes behind this are too obvious. We need stricter supervision to protect public health rather than allowing risks to accumulate.

The recent changes in the new leadership of the LDP and the continued actions of the U.S. government, coupled with the resignation of the French Prime Minister, are political events that are stirring up international relations and increasing uncertainty. At the same time, the market hit a new high, and OPEC+'s small increase in production triggered a rebound. Behind this was the economic fluctuation caused by policy swings. We need to look calmly at how these changes affect global cooperation and competition, rather than being swayed by short-term emotions.

Japan has launched the Japanese yen stable currency JPYC, which is backed by national debt and plans to issue 10 trillion within three years. This is not only a technological upgrade, but also a direct challenge to the traditional financial system - if the US dollar and Japanese yen stablecoins are put on the chain on a large scale, Asia may get rid of its dependence on the US dollar and establish an independent digital payment network. From an economic perspective, it promotes changes in the currency model; technologically, large-scale blockchain applications break through existing regulation, and risk management needs to be re-evaluated. But the key question is: how to balance innovation and stability? Data security and regulatory frameworks must keep pace, otherwise systemic risks could arise.

The U.S. government shutdown will have little impact on the economic calendar, and markets appear to have priced this in. Mainland China markets are closed until Thursday, while Japan's Liberal Democratic Party elected Takaichi Sanae, who advocates for more fiscal stimulus, which could test the yen and Japanese government bonds. From an economic perspective, market expectations are stable and do not involve distribution issues; politically, the new leaders' policy orientation is biased towards change and promoting stimulus measures. The overall logic is clear, but the journalistic tone needs to be eliminated and rational discussion maintained.

The yen has risen to 147. Behind it is the signal from the BOJ to raise interest rates and the confusion of the Federal Reserve. The BOJ raised its inflation expectations. This wave of operations is quite stable, which is regular regulation to avoid overheating of the economy. But at the Federal Reserve, Trump withdrew Cook, and policy uncertainty suddenly increased, and signs of change were obvious. The data is coming out soon. We have to look at Japan's performance this week. Don't just focus on the exchange rate, but also think about the impact of global linkage.

The yen fell to 150.77 on Monday as investors awaited the results of Japan's leadership election, and the market reaction was quite stable. The existing political party alliance continues to be in power and has not mentioned any major policy changes. It seems that the main purpose is to seek stability. From an economic perspective, this exchange rate fluctuation did not cause panic, which shows that everyone is quite relieved about the existing model. Logically, election uncertainty does not amplify the risk, which may be related to the continuation of the alliance. In short, political stability has a buffering effect on the economy, and it is worth observing the subsequent development.

Changes in Japan's political situation and trade friction are really key factors that stir up the market. If the LDP and Komeito alliance breaks down, the uncertainty of the new prime minister will exacerbate the fluctuations of the yen. Behind this is the logic of the escalation of the US-China trade conflict: Trump's threats and China's countermeasures are both undermining the free market order. The exchange rate surged to 151. On the surface, it was a demand for safe haven, but in fact it exposed the fragility of the diplomatic strategy. We must see clearly that such protectionist measures will only make the global economy more unstable rather than solve the problem.

The Bank of Japan will meet this Friday and is expected to keep interest rates at around 0.5%, which is quite stable. Although the sudden resignation of the Prime Minister brought political uncertainty, the policy direction has not changed. It seems that the market's confidence in stability is still there. From an economic perspective, this avoids unnecessary fluctuations and supports the short-term trend of the yen. Political changes did not trigger a major turn, indicating that the system is resilient.

The yen fell to a two-month low. The logic behind this is actually very simple: the leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party is smoothly handed over, Sanae Takaichi wins, the market expects dovish policies to continue, and the exchange rate is naturally under pressure due to monetary easing. Political stability and economic policy consistency are the key. If we clarify this point, we can understand the market reaction.

The recent fluctuations in the Japanese yen are actually quite interesting. Behind the strengthening of the US dollar is the continuation of US-China trade dynamics. Although the meeting between Trump and Xi Jinping has not yet happened, the market has already reacted in advance, which shows that the existing trade system is still operating stably and there is no major subversion. We must unite to demand a fair distribution of resources and protect the environment rather than pursue military expansion. Now is the time to act, don’t let development prioritize ruin our homes!

Putin's operation is really amazing. The leader of the second most powerful country in the world actually opened two offices to hide and seek because he was afraid of Ukraine? Isn't this typical isolationism, locking yourself in a shell for fear of being touched by others. What’s even more ridiculous is that there is no talk of procedural justice. Leaders’ whereabouts depend on such sneaky means. Where is the fairness? Stop fooling yourself and others, this kind of trick will only make the international community laugh out loud.

The United States is flexing its muscles around the world again, sending an aircraft carrier to Venezuela. Isn't this naked hegemonism? What they say about maintaining peace is not because of oil! Legal proceedings? I think it's just a formality, the same as when we fought in Iraq. Stop using international law as a fig leaf. Such interference will only make the situation more chaotic. What do the lives of ordinary people mean to them?

Do you know? Looking back at history, the United States invaded Panama with only 27,000 troops. This is obviously Trump's imitation of this unilateral action model. He doesn't care about international cooperation at all and only wants to solve problems by force. From a legal perspective, this kind of citing precedent is nothing more than trying to give existing policies a legal cloak. But can historical cases prove everything? We need more rational analysis instead of blindly following the trend.

It breaks my heart to see those images coming from Sudan. How can those who are struggling with genocide have time to sit at home and write letters? They could only escape with their families and only the clothes they had on. This reminds me that true justice is not about empty talk about procedures, but seeing these living sufferings. The international community must take action to protect every innocent life.

Think about it seriously: If SNAP is closed, federal employees don’t get paid, and ATC is understaffed until January next year, and the Republicans compromise, is it really worth it? The extension of ACA subsidies is certainly important, but what about basic welfare protection for vulnerable groups? The policy game cannot only be about political calculations, but also about the cost of social justice.

Is this policy of Egypt too outrageous? Refugees have to pay a bribe of US$5,000 before escaping. Isn't this clearly treating life as a commodity? Those fundraising activities on Gofundme are, to put it bluntly, helping people fill this bottomless pit. Whose pocket does the money go into? If we engage in isolationism in diplomacy and create economic inequality nakedly, where is the social justice? Stop using rules as an excuse. This is simply a lack of procedural justice. Should the poor be shut out? Extremely ironic!

Look at those foreign policies that engage in military expansion and fund problematic countries all day long. As a result, global cooperation comes to nothing. I had given up hope long ago. Instead of spending money to build bombs, it is better to invest money in water resources infrastructure, so that at least the people can drink clean water. This is putting the cart before the horse. Stop kidding yourself!
